newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bank of Israel won't cut rates after budget vote.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Israel won't cut rates after budget vote.

text.p: Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel said in an interview published on Friday that he would not lower interest rates after parliament approves the 1997 budget.

"I lowered rates half a percentage point. Don't expect that I will lower interest rates again after approval of the budget by parliament," Frenkel said in an interview in the daily newspaper Yedioth Ahronot.
On Monday, the central bank reduced nominal short-term rates to 14.7 percent from 15.2 percent.

Parliament is now debating the controversial 1997 budget and is expected to approve it by December 31. The budget includes spending cuts, new taxes and other revenue-raising measures totalling more than seven billion shekels aimed at reining in next year's deficit to 2.8 percent of gross domestic product.
Frenkel, however, expressed his dissatisfaction with the budget because it relies too heavily on increased revenues as a substitute for genuine tax cuts.

"When the government increases taxes, or (imposes) tax substitutes, it's not saving anything," he said. "It is only tightening the belts of citizens. It doesn't always succeed and it doesn't always improve the balance of payments, which has a heavy price."
Israel is facing a current account deficit estimated at some $5.4 billion this year, compared with $4.1 billion in 1995.
Frenkel said real interest rates were now at appropriate levels and denied he was using high rates to put pressure on th Treasury to maintain fiscal discipline.
"Non-professionals think the Bank of Israel is maintaining high interest rates to pressure the Treasury, but this is completely incorrect," he said.

"Interest rates are only a means of achieving lower inflation," Frenkel said. "Only when I see that the long-term inflationary trend has really come down and that there is no danger of a renewed outbreak will I go for an additional rate cut."
Frenkel denied that high interest rates were behind the Israeli stock market's slump.

"The most significant contribution the Bank of Israel can make to reviving the stock market is to create an environment of economic stability and confidence," Frenkel said, adding that the real key to resuscitating the market was pension fund reform.
He said the government had to force the funds to invest in traded securities rather than non-tradeable government bonds that make up the lion's share of their assets today.
